summary: The page's arithmetic and data rules (updates per batch, the always-majority accuracy, a blank fill learned from the training rows) work as small Python functions, and its named mistakes with the tape, TensorBoard folders, upload-free loading, fresh-runtime runs and the saved .keras file work as choice questions, while nothing can run TensorFlow, pandas or Colab in the browser runtime.

steps.title: Loading a dataset from code
steps.reason: The four routes need packages and a network, so no Python task fits, and the route names alone are recall. The step still teaches a judgement with named wrong ways: a hand-uploaded file vanishes on a reset and nobody else can rerun it, and a CSV link must open the raw file, not a page that shows it. A choice question on which loading line makes the notebook rerunnable fits.

steps.title: Looking at the data before modelling
steps.reason: The pandas calls do not run in the browser, but the step's point that uneven classes make plain accuracy mislead shows up as a return value: the accuracy of a model that always answers the most common class, about 91% for 5 against not-5 on MNIST. Counting labels with a dict is standard library.

steps.title: Seeds and Runtime > Run all on a fresh runtime
steps.reason: The seed call is TensorFlow's and the check is a Colab menu, so no Python task fits; Python's own random.seed is not taught on the page. The step names three causes a fresh runtime catches (out-of-order cells, a variable from a deleted cell, an uploaded file) and what seeds cannot fix, so a choice question on a Run all that stops with a NameError fits.

steps.title: The test set used once, and a results table kept as you go
steps.reason: The rule that every fill for blanks is learned from the training rows only shows up as a return value: a function that fills blanks in other rows with the mean of the training rows' values. A fill computed over all the rows, the leak the page and the brief name, fails a check.

steps.title: Saving the .keras file, the README and a short deck
steps.reason: Saving and reloading need TensorFlow, and the README table is a convention, but the step names how a hand-in file goes wrong: left in the Colab session it vanishes on a reset, and the path must end in .keras; the check is a reload compared on predictions. A choice question on handing in the saved model fits.

steps.title: What fit does on every batch
steps.reason: TensorFlow is not in the runtime, but the step's count of weight updates (one per batch, a short last batch when the rows do not divide evenly, 422 batches and 844 updates for two epochs) is plain arithmetic a function returns. Floor division (421 batches) and one update per epoch are the wrong readings the page rules out.

steps.title: The same loop written by hand with tf.GradientTape
steps.reason: No check can run a tape in the browser, and the batch slicing is already practised in t1, but the step names a judgement the reader can get wrong: the loss computed outside the with block gives None gradients, while the short last batch, the uncompiled model and training=True are named as harmless here. A choice question on a broken hand loop fits.

steps.title: TensorBoard: comparing two runs
steps.reason: TensorBoard runs only in Colab, so no Python task fits, but the page names what tangles the overlay (a rerun into the same folder) and the fix (one folder per run under one parent, --logdir on the parent), and the brief names reaching for TFLearn. A choice question on one tangled line fits.

tasks.title: What fit does on every batch
tasks.idea: The reader writes count_updates(n_rows, batch_size, epochs), which returns how many times the weights change: one update per batch, with a short last batch when n_rows is not a multiple of batch_size. count_updates(54000, 128, 2) returns 844.
checks: count_updates(54000, 128, 2) returns 844; an answer that drops the short last batch with floor division returns 842.
count_updates(256, 128, 3) returns 6; an answer that always adds one batch for leftover rows returns 9 when the rows divide evenly.
count_updates(54000, 128, 1) returns 422; an answer that counts one update per epoch returns 1.
tasks.q: Write count_updates(n_rows, batch_size, epochs), which returns how many times the weights change when fit trains on n_rows rows for epochs epochs with that batch_size. The weights change once per batch, and when n_rows is not a multiple of batch_size the leftover rows make one last, shorter batch. For example, count_updates(54000, 128, 2) returns 844.
tasks.tests:
assert count_updates(54000, 128, 2) == 844, "the short last batch of each epoch is an update too"
assert count_updates(256, 128, 3) == 6, "rows that divide evenly make no extra batch"
assert count_updates(54000, 128, 1) == 422, "the weights change once per batch, not once per epoch"

tasks.title: The loop written by hand
tasks.idea: A hand-written loop has the forward pass inside with tf.GradientTape() as tape:, but loss = loss_fn(yb, preds) sits on the line after the block, and apply_gradients fails on the first batch. The right answer: the tape never saw the loss, so tape.gradient returns None; move the loss line inside the block.
checks: The last batch holds only 112 rows and breaks the loop, so add code for it: catches missing the page's point that a numpy slice past the end stops at the end and the loop needs no special code.
The model was never compiled, so call compile before the loop: catches the page's line that a hand loop trains an uncompiled model and compile is needed only for evaluate and fit.
The forward pass lacks training=True, so add it: catches the page's note that the flag changes the output only for layers such as Dropout and BatchNormalization, which this network does not have.
tasks.q: A hand-written loop for the 784-128-10 network runs preds = loop_model(xb) inside with tf.GradientTape() as tape:, but loss = loss_fn(yb, preds) sits on the line after the block ends. apply_gradients fails on the first batch. What is wrong?
options: The last batch holds only 112 rows, so the loop needs extra code to handle that short batch.
The model was never compiled, so call compile on it before the loop starts.
The tape never saw the loss, so tape.gradient returns None; move the loss line inside the block.
The forward pass lacks training=True, so add it to the loop_model call.
tasks.explain: The tape records only what runs inside its with block, so it never saw a loss computed after the block and tape.gradient returns None. A hand loop can train an uncompiled model, and training=True changes nothing here, since this network has no Dropout or BatchNormalization layer.

tasks.title: TensorBoard: comparing two runs
tasks.idea: After a change, the plain fit is run again with log_dir="logs/compare/plain", and the Scalars tab now shows one tangled line where two runs were expected. The right answer: the second run's events landed on top of the first; give each run its own folder under logs/compare and point --logdir at the parent.
checks: Add histogram_freq=1 so TensorBoard separates the runs: catches confusing the weight histograms the setting writes with keeping runs apart, which is the folder's job.
Rebuild the model in TFLearn with tensorboard_verbose=3: catches the brief's pitfall of reaching for TFLearn from an old tutorial, which is unmaintained and does not import on Colab's TensorFlow.
Restart the runtime so the old events clear and run again: catches the page's warning that the logs folder disappears when the runtime resets, which loses both runs rather than separating them.
tasks.q: After a change to the plain network, you rerun its fit with its callback's log_dir still "logs/compare/plain". TensorBoard, opened with --logdir logs/compare, now draws the plain run as one tangled line where you expected the old and new runs as two. What fixes it?
options: Raise the callback's histogram_freq, so TensorBoard can tell the two runs apart.
Rebuild the network in TFLearn with tensorboard_verbose=3, so each run logs on its own.
Restart the Colab runtime so the old events clear, then run the changed fit once more.
Give each run its own folder under logs/compare, so the rerun no longer writes on top of the first.
tasks.explain: Rerunning a fit into the same folder adds the second run's events on top of the first, so one line turns into a tangle. With one folder per run under one parent, and --logdir on that parent, the Scalars tab draws each run as its own line; histogram_freq only sets how often the weights' histograms are written.

tasks.title: Loading a dataset from code
tasks.idea: A notebook reads pd.read_csv("penguins.csv") from a file uploaded by hand into Colab, and a reviewer cannot rerun it. The right answer: read the CSV from the URL of the raw file with pd.read_csv(url), so the data loads from code on any runtime.
checks: Pass pd.read_csv the address of the web page that shows the table: catches the page's rule that the link must open the raw file itself, not a page that displays it.
Keep the upload and add a README line asking the reviewer to upload the same file: catches the page's point that nobody else can rerun a notebook that needs a hand-uploaded file.
Upload the file once more and leave it in the session: catches the page's point that a hand-uploaded file disappears when the runtime resets.
tasks.q: A notebook's loading cell reads pd.read_csv("penguins.csv") from a file its author uploaded by hand into Colab, and a reviewer cannot rerun the notebook. What change lets anyone rerun it?
options: Read the CSV with pd.read_csv(url), where url opens the raw file itself.
Pass pd.read_csv the address of the web page that shows the table.
Keep the upload, and add a README line asking the reviewer to upload the same file.
Upload the file once more and leave it sitting in the Colab session for later runs.
tasks.explain: A notebook that loads its data from code runs anywhere, and pd.read_csv reads a CSV straight from a web address when the link opens the raw file, not a page that shows it. A file uploaded by hand disappears when the runtime resets.

tasks.title: Looking at the data
tasks.idea: The reader writes majority_accuracy(labels), which returns, as a fraction, the accuracy of a model that always answers the most common label in the list. For the penguins' species, 152 Adelie, 124 Gentoo and 68 Chinstrap, it returns 152 / 344, about 0.44.
checks: On a list with one "5" and ten "not 5" labels it returns 10 / 11; an answer that scores the rare class returns 1 / 11, missing how a model that ignores the rare class still scores high.
On the penguin counts it returns 152 / 344, a fraction; an answer that returns the count 152 is not an accuracy.
When the most common label appears last in the list it is still the one counted; an answer that takes the first label's count returns the wrong fraction.
tasks.q: Write majority_accuracy(labels). labels is a list of class labels, one per row, and the function returns, as a fraction between 0 and 1, the accuracy of a model that always answers the most common label in the list. For example, for the penguins' species, 152 "Adelie", 124 "Gentoo" and 68 "Chinstrap", it returns 152 / 344, about 0.44.
tasks.tests:
assert majority_accuracy(["5"] + ["not 5"] * 10) == 10 / 11, "always answering the common class still scores high when one class is rare"
assert majority_accuracy(["Adelie"] * 152 + ["Gentoo"] * 124 + ["Chinstrap"] * 68) == 152 / 344, "returns the share of rows answered right, not a count"
assert majority_accuracy(["Gentoo", "Chinstrap", "Adelie", "Adelie", "Adelie"]) == 3 / 5, "finds the most common label wherever it sits in the list"

tasks.title: Seeds and Run all
tasks.idea: A notebook runs fine in its author's session. After a cell that made scaler was deleted, Runtime > Run all on a fresh runtime stops with a NameError on scaler. The right answer: a later cell used a variable left over from the deleted cell; put the cell that makes it back above its first use and run the fresh-runtime check again.
checks: Set the seeds at the top so the run repeats: catches thinking seeds fix any rerun difference, when they only make random choices repeat and create no variable.
Run the cells by hand in the order that worked in the session: catches the page's named cause, cells run out of order, which a fresh Run all exists to catch.
Record the library versions, since Colab's versions changed: catches confusing version drift, which can move numbers, with a missing name, which it does not cause.
tasks.q: A notebook runs fine in its author's session. After the cell that made scaler was deleted, Runtime > Run all on a fresh runtime stops with NameError: name 'scaler' is not defined. What is the fix?
options: Set the seeds in the top cell, so every rerun of the notebook repeats the same way.
Put a cell that makes scaler back above its first use, then Run all on a fresh runtime again.
Run the cells by hand, in the order that worked in the author's session.
Record the library versions in the README, since Colab's preinstalled versions changed.
tasks.explain: On a fresh runtime the only state is what the cells create, top to bottom, so it catches a variable left over from a deleted cell: the cell that makes scaler must sit above the first cell that uses it, and a second fresh Run all proves the fix. Seeds only make random choices repeat, and other library versions can move numbers but do not remove a name.

tasks.title: The test set used once
tasks.idea: The reader writes fill_from_training(train, rows): train and rows are lists of numbers with None for a blank, and the function returns a new list like rows with each None replaced by the mean of train's numbers. fill_from_training([1.0, None, 3.0], [None, 10.0]) returns [2.0, 10.0].
checks: The fill comes from the training rows only; an answer that averages train and rows together, the leak the page names, returns about 4.67 in place of 2.0.
Blanks in train are skipped when the mean is taken; an answer that counts None as 0 or divides by the full length returns a smaller fill.
Numbers in rows pass through unchanged; an answer that replaces every value with the mean loses the 10.0.
tasks.q: Write fill_from_training(train, rows). train and rows are lists of numbers from one column, with None for a blank: train holds the training rows and rows another part of the split. The function returns a list like rows with each None replaced by the mean of the numbers in train, its blanks left out, and with the numbers already in rows as they were. For example, fill_from_training([1.0, None, 3.0], [None, 10.0]) returns [2.0, 10.0].
tasks.tests:
assert fill_from_training([1.0, None, 3.0], [None, 10.0]) == [2.0, 10.0], "the fill is the mean of the training rows only"
assert fill_from_training([2.0, None, None, 4.0], [None]) == [3.0], "blanks in the training rows are left out of the mean"
assert fill_from_training([1.0, 3.0], [4.0, None, 10.0]) == [4.0, 2.0, 10.0], "numbers already in rows stay as they were"

tasks.title: Saving the .keras file
tasks.idea: A notebook ends with the kept model trained, and the hand-in is the saved model. The right answer: kept.save("digits_kept.keras"), reload it with tf.keras.models.load_model, check the predictions on the same rows agree with np.allclose, then download the file.
checks: Save it and leave it in the Colab session's files for the reviewer: catches the page's warning that Colab loses the file when the runtime resets, so it must be downloaded.
Save it to a path with no .keras ending, such as digits_kept: catches the page's rule that the path must end in .keras.
tasks.q: Your notebook ends with the kept model, kept, trained, and the hand-in is the saved model. Which way of handing it in works?
options: Save it with kept.save("digits_kept.keras") and leave the file in the session's files, where the reviewer can open it and check it loads.
Save it with kept.save("digits_kept"), a name with no file ending, check it loads back, then download that file.
Save it with kept.save("digits_kept.keras"), check that tf.keras.models.load_model gives the same predictions on the same rows, then download the file.
tasks.explain: model.save needs a path that ends in .keras, and predictions that agree on the same rows after a reload with tf.keras.models.load_model show the file holds the whole trained model. Colab loses the file when the runtime resets, so the downloaded copy is the hand-in.
